clue.text: Meadow -he's turned over by ancient tenure

indicators.note: something turned over is flipped end to end, so the word it follows is read backwards

blocks.note: lea is a poetic word for a meadow
taken as written, then turned round
ancient means very old

explanation.surface: A field held under some archaic system of land tenure, its owner overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces run LEA + SEH + OLD; 'by' simply places one piece beside the next.
explanation.definitionFit: A leasehold is a form of property tenure, holding land or a building under a lease for a fixed term.

clue.text: This number could be, three

indicators.note: 'could be' suggests one possible form among several, so the letters can be put in another order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A puzzle about which figure might be three.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' reads as a figure but means something that numbs, pronounced with the B: ether was an early anaesthetic.
explanation.definitionFit: Ether was used as a general anaesthetic, a substance that deadens feeling, so it is a numbing agent.

clue.text: e.g. Lancing some whales

blocks.note: first meaning: Lancing College is a boarding ... in Sussex, England
second meaning: the collective noun for a group of whales or fish

explanation.surface: Harpooners lancing a few whales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lancing' looks like a verb about spearing whales, but it is the name of an English independent school.
explanation.definitionFit: Lancing College is an independent school, and a group of whales swimming together is called a school or pod.

clue.text: Part of New York initially housing a real live ethnic minority

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so each following word gives up only its opening letter

blocks.clueFragment: housing a real live ethnic minority
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of the six words

explanation.surface: A district of New York that first housed a lively ethnic community.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay also describes the place: the Manhattan neighbourhood long home to a large African American community.
explanation.definitionFit: Harlem is a neighbourhood in northern Manhattan, one of the boroughs of New York City.

clue.text: Guides, we hear, in place for contending pianists

indicators.note: what we hear is a spoken sound, so the word is judged by pronunciation not spelling

blocks.note: to guide is to lead; said aloud this matches the city

explanation.surface: Musicians being guided into a competition venue.
explanation.walkthrough: The Leeds International Piano Competition, held in the Yorkshire city every three years, is a major contest for young pianists.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern English city hosts a famous international piano competition, so it is where pianists compete.

clue.text: Chemical lot OK for mixing it can be sold in bars

definitions.text: it can be sold in bars

indicators.note: mixing stirs ingredients together, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A chemical batch approved for blending into something sold in bars, as if it were a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' suggests pubs selling a mixed drink; here they are slabs of confectionery.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk chocolate is commonly sold as slabs or bars of confectionery, so it is something sold in bars.

clue.text: Producing coal for bonfire Caruso put out

indicators.note: someone put out is upset and disturbed, so the words before are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Fetching coal for a bonfire that the tenor Caruso extinguished.
explanation.walkthrough: Enrico Caruso was a famous Italian opera tenor. 'Put out' looks like extinguishing the bonfire.
explanation.definitionFit: Carboniferous means coal-bearing, and names the geological period when most of the world's coal seams formed.

clue.text: Mobile soldier up by day?

blocks.note: surface reading: a soldier on the move who gets out of bed in the daytime
setter's reading: a mounted cavalryman, 'up' in the saddle, and 'by day' points to light rather than dark

explanation.surface: A soldier on the move who rises with the daylight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' means mounted on a horse, and daytime is the light part of the day, so a light cavalryman fits both halves.
explanation.definitionFit: Light cavalry were lightly armed mounted troops used for scouting and raiding, so their riders were highly mobile soldiers.

clue.text: Random investigation for measles patient?

blocks.note: first meaning: an unannounced check on a sample
second meaning, whimsical: an examination of someone's rash of red spots

explanation.surface: A random test carried out on someone who has measles.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second half as a pun: a doctor checking a measles patient literally checks the spots.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot check is an unannounced inspection of a random sample, made on the spot without warning.

clue.text: Money and job needed for one at this level of subsistence

definitions.text: one at this level of subsistence

blocks.note: bread is slang for money
one's line is one's line of work

explanation.surface: Money and work are what anyone living at a bare subsistence level needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone 'on the breadline' is very poor, living at the lowest level of subsistence, near starvation.

clue.text: Game for standing at fireside

blocks.note: first meaning: a card game played for stakes
second meaning: the metal rod kept by the hearth for stirring the coals

explanation.surface: A party game played while everyone stands round the fire.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a betting card game and the iron rod used to stir a coal fire, which stands beside the grate.

clue.text: Senior takes in order that is not drunk

indicators.note: to take something in is to receive it inside, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: Sr is the usual abbreviation for senior
the Order of the British Empire, an honour

explanation.surface: An elderly man accepts an honour while remaining clear-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: The OBE (Officer of the Order of the British Empire) is a British honour, a standard crossword 'order'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sober describes someone with no alcohol in their system, the plain opposite of intoxicated.

clue.text: This beast of burden has a straight drive back

indicators.note: going back runs the wrong way, so the phrase before it is read from its end

blocks.note: taken as written
The Mall is the long straight avenue leading to Buckingham Palace

explanation.surface: A pack animal taking a straight path home, or a cricketer's straight drive hit back.
explanation.walkthrough: A + MALL read backwards gives the animal; 'straight drive' sounds like cricket but is a road. The Mall is a ceremonial avenue in London.
explanation.definitionFit: The llama is a South American camelid long kept by Andean peoples for carrying loads.

clue.text: Sign of the pound being up?

definitions.text: Sign of the pound being up?

blocks.note: surface reading: an indication that sterling is rising on the currency markets
setter's reading: a star sign up in the heavens, named for the scales and the Latin word for a pound weight

explanation.surface: An indicator that sterling is gaining in value.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin word for a pound weight is also the zodiac sign of the scales, and the abbreviations lb and the £ symbol come from it.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventh zodiac sign is the Scales, and its Latin name originally meant a Roman pound weight.

clue.text: Confuse with a heavy blow

blocks.note: taken as written
a bash is a hard knock

explanation.surface: Knocking someone senseless with a heavy punch.
explanation.definitionFit: To abash is to disconcert or embarrass someone, leaving them flustered and confused.

clue.text: Girl with silver head, almost ...

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of it, so the word just before loses its final letter

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A girl going grey, almost, her sentence trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' suggests hair, but it is a promontory. The dots lead on to 22-down, whose answer is another girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnes is a female first name, so it names a girl.

clue.text: Destination of Bounty — it came back holding a strike

indicators.note: coming back is travelling in the opposite direction, so the short word is turned round
holding something means having it inside your grasp, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then turned round
taken as written
to strike is to hit

explanation.surface: A ship's voyage ends in mutiny: it returns after a strike by the crew.
explanation.walkthrough: TI wraps round A HIT. HMS Bounty, of the famous mutiny, sailed to this island to collect breadfruit plants.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bounty's 1787 voyage was bound for the Polynesian island to gather breadfruit, making it the ship's goal.

clue.text: Old coin to us, new to Pacific island

blocks.note: first meaning: a former British gold coin worth twenty-one shillings
second meaning: put 'New' in front and you have the large island north of Australia

explanation.surface: A coin long gone from British pockets is still novel currency on some Pacific island.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is cryptic: the word needs 'New' before it to name the island, which is what 'new to' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: The guinea was an old British coin, and New Guinea is the big island in the western Pacific.

clue.text: Mind it leaving Britain?

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so those letters drop out of the word that follows

blocks.note: taken as written; these are the letters removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Would you mind if it left Britain? A worry about something emigrating.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove IT from BRITAIN and BRAIN is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Brain and mind are used interchangeably for a person's intellect or capacity to think.

clue.text: Son of King Priam—bully for him!

blocks.note: first meaning: the Trojan prince, eldest son of Priam, killed by Achilles
second meaning: to browbeat or intimidate

explanation.surface: Cheering a Trojan prince: 'Bully for him!' as an exclamation of praise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bully for him' reads as one exclamation, but 'bully' is a verb meaning the answer and 'for him' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: The greatest Trojan warrior in the Iliad was Priam's son, and his name became an English verb for blustering intimidation.

clue.text: Feel free if inside tower

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and may settle in any arrangement
something put inside sits within another piece, so one goes into the other

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to feel unconstrained when you are shut inside a tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feel free' reads as an invitation, but 'free' is the anagram signal working on 'Feel'. The definition names the tower by its surname, as in the Eiffel Tower.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eiffel Tower in Paris is the most famous tower in the world, so its name alone can stand for a tower.

clue.text: Glowing prize of English sport

blocks.note: surface reading: a shining trophy that English sportsmen compete for
setter's reading: the burnt remains of a fire, which glow, and the cricket trophy of the same name fought over by England and Australia

explanation.surface: A gleaming trophy that English sportsmen chase.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket series between England and Australia is played for a tiny urn said to hold a burnt bail; embers left by a fire still glow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Test cricket trophy contested by England and Australia carries this name, after a mock obituary for English cricket in 1882.

clue.text: . . Sydney's girl?

blocks.note: surface reading: the girlfriend of a man named Sydney, continuing the girl of the previous clue
setter's reading: a girl from the Australian city, called by the local slang word

explanation.surface: A man called Sydney's girlfriend, following on from the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Sydney looks like a man's name, but it is the Australian city.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang a woman or girl is a sheila, so a girl from that city is one.

clue.text: Unrefined ground by end of January

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the ground is the earth
its final letter

explanation.surface: Coarse powder milled by the end of January.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a past tense of grind, but it is soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy describes coarse, crude or down-to-earth behaviour, lacking polish or refinement.

clue.text: Eastern ruler of only half a state

indicators.note: keeping only half of something throws the rest away, so the back half of the word goes

blocks.note: an American state of ten letters

explanation.surface: An oriental potentate who rules only half of his country.
explanation.walkthrough: Of a ten-letter state, keep the first five letters. Calif is a variant spelling of caliph.
explanation.definitionFit: A caliph was the civil and religious ruler of a Muslim state, a title from the Middle East, here spelt calif.

clue.text: One aspect of ice-cutting?

blocks.note: surface reading: a single feature of chopping up ice
setter's reading: ice is slang for diamonds, and a cut gem has many flat polished faces

explanation.surface: Something to consider about breaking up ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice' is old slang for diamonds, so ice-cutting is gem-cutting.
explanation.definitionFit: A facet is both one aspect of a matter and one of the flat faces ground onto a cut diamond.

clue.text: Dangerous sea-nymph shows anger in two ways

indicators.note: something in another thing sits within it, so one piece lies between the others

blocks.note: two compass directions, south and north
ire is a literary word for anger

explanation.surface: A perilous sea creature flies into a rage in two different ways.
explanation.walkthrough: S and N stand for two compass points, and IRE goes between them.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the sirens were sea creatures whose singing lured sailors to wreck on the rocks.

clue.text: Gleaming brightness observed round hospital

indicators.note: going round something encircles it, so one piece is wrapped about the other

blocks.note: observed means seen
H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A shining glow noticed around a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheen is a soft lustre or shine on a surface, a gleaming kind of brightness.

clue.text: Slough post for staid conservative?

blocks.note: a post is a stake or pole
a slough is a bog or swamp, so a post in a slough stands in mire

explanation.surface: A job in the town of Slough for a dull conservative type.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough looks like the Berkshire town and 'post' like a job, but a slough is a bog and the post is a stake planted there.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone dull and resistant to change, matching a stuffy, staid traditionalist.

clue.text: Gent Daisy reformed, preventing wobble

indicators.note: something reformed has been made over into a new shape, so the letters before it are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A man and a woman named Daisy, reformed characters, keep things on an even keel.
explanation.definitionFit: Steadying something means making it firm and balanced, which stops it rocking or wobbling.
